# Best Postgres hosting for SaaS and AI agents (2026)

Compare Neon, Amazon RDS, DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL, and Supabase for SaaS and AI agents on price, branching, functions, and AI gateways.

A growing share of Postgres databases aren't long-running production apps. They're previews, experiments, and apps an AI agent built in a few minutes, and many of them become idle soon. AI agents now create over 80% of the databases on Neon.

On a host that bills each database as an always-on instance, every one of those copies costs as much as production, whether anyone uses it or not. And a copy of the database alone isn't enough, because the app also needs its files, its users, and its backend code.

This guide compares five Postgres hosts on what those databases cost, from idle apps to short-lived copies of production, and on how each host copies the rest of the backend along with the data, so developers and agents can iterate faster.

## What do you need from Postgres hosting?

At a minimum, Postgres hosting for a modern app should give you:

- Managed Postgres with backups, point-in-time restore, and connection pooling.
- Predictable pricing you can estimate before your app grows.
- A usable free tier to build and test a real app before you pay.

For teams that open many pull requests and agents that run many experiments, the options that stand out add:

- Branching with data: A pull request or agent run gets a copy of production data in under a second, without a dump and restore.
- Object storage that branches too: Files uploaded or generated by your app are copied into each branch along with the rows that reference them.
- Functions that branch too: Backend code deploys to each branch and runs next to its data, so a preview or agent run tests the code and the database together.
- A built-in AI gateway: One credential for models from several providers, so each branch can test a new model or prompt without a new API key.
- Usage-based billing: Idle preview and experiment environments cost little or nothing.

Let's quickly see how the five options compare on price before we go deeper:

# Managed Postgres pricing in 2026: eight providers compared

What a 1 GB and a 4 GB managed Postgres cost on Ownkube, Heroku, Railway, DigitalOcean, Render, Neon, Supabase and Fly.io, with list prices checked 2026-10-13.

Abhishek Jaiswal

 Oct 14, 2026 · 7 min 

Managed Postgres is priced in more ways than almost any other cloud product. Some providers sell a fixed instance with storage on top, some include storage up to a cap, one meters memory by the hour, and one wraps the database in a $25 platform plan. That makes two quotes hard to compare at a glance.

This post prices the same two databases on eight providers, using list prices read from each provider’s pricing page on 2026-10-13. The numbers match our managed Postgres cost calculator, where you can try any size.

TL;DR

- For a small database (1 GB of memory, 10 GB of storage), monthly prices run from $9 on Heroku Essential-1 to about $41 on Fly.io Managed Postgres. Ownkube is $10.50.
- For a mid-size database (4 GB of memory, 50 GB of storage), the range runs from $40.50 on Ownkube to $296 on Fly.io, which has no plan between 2 GB and 8 GB.
- Heroku’s Essential plans are the cheapest small option, with shared memory and a hard 10 GB storage cap on Essential-1.
- Neon and Railway bill by usage, so a quiet database costs less than the always-on figures here. Fly.io includes high availability in every plan, which is part of why it costs more.

## How do providers price managed Postgres?

Across the eight providers we found four pricing models.

### Fixed instance plus storage

You pick a memory size and pay a flat monthly price, then pay per GB of disk. Ownkube, Render and Fly.io work this way.

### Fixed instance with storage included

The plan price covers a set amount of disk. Heroku includes storage up to each plan’s cap. DigitalOcean includes the low end of a storage range and charges for more in 10 GiB steps.

### Usage-based

Neon bills compute in CU-hours (one CU is about 4 GB of memory) plus storage. Railway bills memory and CPU by the minute plus volume storage.

### Platform plan plus compute

Supabase Pro costs $25 a month and includes $10 of compute credit and 8 GB of disk. Larger compute sizes and extra disk add to that.

The storage rate is easy to skim past. It ranges from $0.125 per GB on Supabase to $0.35 per GB on Neon, which matters more as the database grows.

# Where to host Postgres in 2026: RDS, Neon, Supabase and 20 more

Maxine Verbose· Infrastructure · Tuesday, 20 October 2026

What the smallest Postgres instance costs per month and what it costs to scale, on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale and 17 more, from serverless to self-hosting. Plus upgrade downtime, versions, extensions, HA, backups, pooling and rules for picking one.

Picking a Postgres host looks like a price comparison, and prices do differ tenfold for the same database. The costly surprises come later: a restore that overwrites the database in place, HA that turns out to be an alpha, a provider still on Postgres 17, backups you can’t download, or an exit that means a `pg_dump` over metered egress.

This guide answers the two price questions first: what the smallest instance costs and what each step up costs. Then it compares 23 hosted options, plus self-hosting, on the features that decide the rest.

All prices come from the vendors’ own pricing pages, price APIs and docs, read on 20 October 2026; versions and features were read on 19 October. We didn’t run or benchmark any of these services; every latency or failover figure is the vendor’s own.

## The short answer

- Side project: Neon’s free plan, or Supabase’s if you also want auth and storage (it pauses after a week idle and caps the database at 500 MB of storage).
- Startup app: Neon Launch for a database only ($0.106 per CU-hour; 2 GB RAM never sleeping is $38.69 a month plus storage), Supabase Pro for the bundled backend ($30 a month with 2 GB RAM), or PlanetScale if you want a hot standby from day one ($50 for a three-node cluster with 2 GiB RAM each).
- Serverless or edge app: Neon; Prisma Postgres if you use Prisma and run few queries; on AWS, Aurora Serverless v2 if a 15-second resume is acceptable.
- AI app needing pgvector: every host but Aurora DSQL has it, at versions 0.8.1 to 0.8.6 (current: 0.8.7).
- Heavy analytics or time series: Tiger Cloud for full TimescaleDB, or AlloyDB’s columnar engine on Google Cloud.
- Regulated workload (HIPAA): AWS, Google Cloud or Azure under the cloud’s BAA, PlanetScale, whose plans include BAAs, or Neon’s Scale plan, which includes HIPAA at no extra cost for now (Neon plans a 15% surcharge).
- Lowest fixed price: PlanetScale’s $5 PS-5 node (512 MiB RAM, 10 GB storage included). With 2 GB of RAM: Azure’s burstable B1ms ($12 plus storage, not meant for production), PlanetScale’s PS-20 ($17, 10 GB storage included), Ubicloud’s hobby-1 ($18 plus storage) or a $20 Hetzner server you run yourself (40 GB storage included).
- Shortest upgrade downtime: for a major upgrade of a single-primary database, RDS or Aurora with Blue/Green (a switchover typically under a minute) or Crunchy Bridge (a few minutes, set by object count rather than data size); multi-node CockroachDB and YugabyteDB clusters stay up.
